en: The Extremely Rare Sūtra, translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang, Xuanzang, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Rājagṛha, dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as immeasurable bodhisattvas, devas, humans, and others.

At that time, in the early part of the day, the Venerable Ānanda, for the purpose of begging for food, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha, proceeding from house to house to beg for alms.
From afar, he saw a great multi-storied pavilion, its construction recently completed, adorned with exquisite and magnificent decorations, exceedingly lovely and delightful.
Having seen this, he reflected within himself:

"If there were good sons or good daughters who could construct such a high and wide pavilion, adorned with exquisite and magnificent decorations, exceedingly lovely and delightful, and offer it as a gift to the Sangha of Great Virtues of the four directions."

Furthermore, there may be sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, erect stūpas even as small as an *āmra* fruit, placing within them a *dhātu* of the Buddha no larger than a mustard seed; they raise a banner-pole (*yaṣṭi*) like a large needle, with a *cakra* finial atop it like a small jujube leaf, or they fashion images of the Buddha no smaller than a grain of wild barley.
"Between these two kinds of merit produced, which is greater?
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda had this thought: having gone on alms-round sequentially through the city of Rājagṛha, he was returning to his own quarters.
Having finished his meal, put away his robes and bowl, and washed his feet, he went to where the Tathāgata was at the time after eating.
Upon arrival, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Just now, at the first part of the day, for the sake of alms, I put on my robes and took up my bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in regular order.

From afar, I saw a certain great multi-storied pavilion, its construction recently completed, adorned with exquisite and magnificent decorations, most delightful to behold. Having seen it, I reflected within myself:

'If there were some sons or daughters of good family who could construct such a high and wide multi-storied pavilion, adorned with exquisite and magnificent decorations, most delightful to behold, and offer it as a gift to the Great Virtuous Saṃgha of the four quarters;'"

Furthermore, there may be sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, erect stūpas even as small as an *āmala* fruit, placing within them a relic (*buddhadhātu*) no larger than a mustard seed; they erect a pinnacle (*yasti*) like a large needle, with a *cakra* (wheel) on top like a small jujube leaf; or they fashion images of the Buddha no larger than a grain of hulled barley.
"Between these two kinds of merit produced, which is greater?
Therefore, I now inquire of the World-Honored One; I only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on me and explain it."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda with his wondrous Brahma-voice: "Excellent, excellent!

Desiring now to bring benefit and peace to immeasurable sentient beings, and out of compassion for the devas and humans of the world so that they may attain great purpose, benefit, peace, and happiness, you have questioned the Tathāgata regarding such a profound matter."
"Listen attentively now and reflect well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:

"Right here, in this region of Jambudvīpa, it is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a carriage box, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise."

Suppose that within this space they were joined together into a single mass—whether a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, or a bamboo forest, or perhaps fields of rice or sesame—packed so densely as to leave no intervening gaps.

Suppose, for instance, that the entire continent of Jambudvīpa were filled to capacity with those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhats, or pratyekabuddhas, packed so densely together without any intervening space, like stalks of sugarcane.

Suppose there is a single family that, throughout their entire lives, reverently serves and makes offerings to that assembly of noble ones, presenting them with excellent robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessary requisites; and after each one has entered parinirvāṇa, they cremate their bodies according to the Dharma, collect their remains, and erect a stūpa—high, vast, and magnificently adorned—offering praise and worship with ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners, canopies, precious standards, music, and the light of lamps and torches.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

“Setting aside this continent of Jambudvīpa in the south, consider here in the east the continent of Pūrvavideha, which is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, shaped like a half-moon, and the faces of its people are likewise.”

Suppose that within this space they were joined together as a single mass—whether a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, or a forest of bamboo, or perhaps fields of rice or sesame—packed so densely that there was no intervening gap.

Suppose, for instance, that the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha were entirely filled with those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or Arhats, or Pratyekabuddhas, packed so closely together without any gaps, like stalks of sugarcane.

Suppose there is a family that, throughout their entire lives, reveres, serves, and makes offerings to that assembly of noble ones, presenting them with the finest robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessary requisites. After each of those individuals has entered parinirvāṇa, they cremate their bodies according to the Dharma, collect their remains, and erect stūpas—lofty, vast, and magnificently adorned—offering praise and worship with ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners, canopies, precious standards, music, and the radiant light of lamps and torches.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

“Setting aside the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, consider this western continent of Aparagoyānī, which is nine thousand yojanas in length, breadth, and circumference, shaped like a solar disc, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise.”

Suppose that within this space were formed a single continuous mass—whether a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, a bamboo forest, or even fields of rice and sesame—packed so densely together that there was no intervening gap.

Suppose, for instance, that the entire western continent of Aparagoyānī were completely filled with those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas, packed so densely without any intervening space, like stalks of sugarcane.

Suppose there is a single family that, throughout their entire lives, reverently serves, attends to, and makes offerings to that assembly of noble ones; they present them with superior and exquisite robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various requisites. After each of those individuals has entered parinirvāṇa, they cremate their bodies according to the Dharma, collect their remains, and erect stūpas—high, vast, and magnificently adorned—with ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, excellent banners, canopies, precious standards, music, and the light of lamps and torches, offering praise and worship.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

“Setting aside the western continent of Aparagoyānī for a moment, consider this northern continent of Uttarakuru, which is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with a square terrain and human faces likewise shaped as squares.”

Suppose that within this space were formed a single continuous mass—whether a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, a bamboo forest, or even fields of rice or sesame—packed so densely that there was no intervening gap.

In this way, even if the entire northern continent of Uttarakuru were filled to capacity with those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas, packed so closely together that there is no space between them, like stalks of sugarcane; [the merit would still be surpassed by that of one who hears this Dharma].

Suppose there is a single family that, throughout their entire lives, reverently serves and makes offerings to those noble ones, presenting them with excellent clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various necessities; and after each of those individuals has entered parinirvāṇa, they cremate their bodies according to the Dharma, collect their remains, and erect stūpas—tall, wide, and magnificently adorned—offering praise and worship with ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners, canopies, precious pennants, music, and the light of lamps and torches.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

“Setting aside for a moment the great continent of Uttarakuru in the north, the Lord of Devas, Śakra, possesses a great tiered terrace. This terrace rests upon eighty-four thousand exquisite pillars of various jewels. Each jewel pillar is encased with nets of various celestial blue lapis lazuli, exquisite gems, and pearls; it is strewn with golden sand and sprinkled with scented water.”

This terrace was surrounded on all sides by eighty-four thousand windows made of exquisite jewels; from each and every window hung various celestial lapis lazuli, wonderful gems, and pearl curtains, strewn with golden dust and sprinkled with scented water.

This terrace further possesses eighty-four thousand exquisite jewel pavilions; each pavilion is covered with various celestial blue lapis lazuli, wonderful jewels, and pearl nets, strewn with golden sand, and sprinkled with scented water.

Suppose there were some sons of good family or daughters of good family who constructed a magnificent multi-storied pavilion, high, vast, and splendidly adorned, resembling the exquisite jeweled terrace of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and offered it as a gift to the assembly of virtuous monks of the four directions.
"What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on account of this cause and condition?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:

“Setting aside the four continents and the great precious tiered terrace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, suppose there were some sons or daughters of good family who could construct hundreds of thousands of koṭis of tiered pavilions—high, broad, magnificent, and beautiful—all like Śakra’s wonderful precious tiered terrace—and offer them to the assembly of the Great Virtuous Saṃgha of the four directions.”

Furthermore, there may be sons of good family or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of various Tathāgatas, erect stūpas even as small as an *āmala* fruit, placing within them a relic (*buddhadhātu*) the size of a mustard seed; they set up a banner pole (*yasti*) as thin as a large needle, with a parasol (*cakra*) atop it like a small jujube leaf, or they fashion an image of the Buddha even as small as a grain of hulled barley.

If one were to compare that previous mass of merit with this mass of merit, it would not equal even a hundredth part of it; it would not equal even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical part, nor a calculable part, nor a fraction, nor a metaphorical part, nor even a part comparable to the *upaniṣad*.

Why is this? Ānanda! Although the measure of the aforementioned mass of merit is vast, it does not equal that which results from the fact that all Tathāgatas, throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, have cultivated and accumulated immeasurable superior morality, concentration, and wisdom, as well as liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation, all of which they have brought to perfection.

Because the Tathāgata’s immeasurable loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as his teachings and supernatural powers throughout the ten directions and across the six realms of existence, are all perfected; and because the Tathāgata’s immeasurable generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and all other virtues are likewise perfected.
"By this you should know that the mass of merit obtained from fashioning images of the Buddha and stūpas is inconceivable and beyond comparison.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"You should reverently receive such a Dharma-gate."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“I have respectfully accepted it.
I do not yet know the name of this Dharma-gate thus taught; what should I call it so that I may uphold it?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Dharma-gate is named 'Exceedingly Rare'; it enables sentient beings to plant all perfectly pure and white dharmas. You should uphold it by this name."

Ānanda, you should know that since the distant past, I have repeatedly and extensively expounded this Dharma gate for devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even for humans and non-humans, proclaiming and revealing it to them.
For what reason?

It is because the World-Honored One desires that such classes of sentient beings as these may cultivate various roots of goodness through unerring reverence toward the Tathāgata, thereby obtaining benefit and peace for a long night and swiftly attaining unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment.

When the Blessed One had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the great assembly of bhikṣus, immeasurable bodhisattvas, as well as the devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Extremely Rare Sūtra (Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra)
